# Putting data to good use {#gooduse}

## Failure mode

We hope to have shown that the data in @WalkdenEa2023 do not provide strong evidence for the authors' claims --- though the authors plainly believe they do. How did that happen? The shape of the mistake is by now familiar. A loosely specified theory (Section \@ref(hypotheses)) was asked to draw support from a chain of derivations --- substantive tenets to particular predictions to statistical hypotheses to Nulls of the form "*variable V has no influence*" --- and a positive inference was then run all the way back up the chain, from "the Null is rejected" to "Trudgill's theory is corroborated and our method works." Each step treated every auxiliary hypothesis in the network as true and every rejected Null as a finding.

The chain breaks at both ends. At the top, the loose fit of an informal theory means even a clean rejection transmits almost nothing upward: the test had no real capacity to find the theory wrong, so passing it is not severity but coincidence (Section \@ref(testing)). At the bottom, the rejections themselves are unsound --- products of NHST applied to aggregated, unweighted scores --- so there is nothing to transmit in the first place. Two heroic inferences stacked on a foundation that does not hold: the result is not a modest finding, or a weak one, but no finding at all. We can only speculate why none of this was caught --- by the authors, the editors, or the reviewers. Rather than dwell there, we offer three things that would help, none of them ours: other fields have met the same problems and thought hard about them.

## Remedy 1: disciplined inference and better theories

Be modest about what an inference can carry. Testing is piecemeal, and any one study should aim at the most specific corner of the hypothesis network it can actually reach, not the grand theory above it. The deeper fix, though, is on the theory side: linguistic theories would be far more testable if they predicted *numbers* --- at minimum a numerical range the measurements should fall in. That is what sharpens a particular hypothesis into something a test can genuinely fail. Where a research tradition measures the same thing repeatedly, those ranges can also come from meta-analysis [see @Vasishth2015 for a psycholinguistic example].

With numerical expectations in hand, one can test using Neyman--Pearson logic [@NeymanPearson1933; @Neyman1937; @Neyman1957] or severity [@MayoSpanos2004] and earn a real positive inference, rather than merely rejecting an uninformative Null. But we should be honest about the catch, because it bears directly on the case at hand: principled confirmatory testing needs not only numerical predictions but data of sufficient quantity, control, and quality to put them at risk. Historical-corpus data of the kind Walkden et al. work with will, in all likelihood, never meet that bar --- there simply are not, and never will be, enough well-controlled texts from the right places and centuries. Recognising when the data cannot bear *any* confirmatory framework is itself part of disciplined inference. The answer is not to run Neyman--Pearson harder; it is to stop forcing data into a confirmatory mould they were never going to fill --- a point we return to at the close.

And, frankly, the field needs better statistical training. If you have read this far and felt the analysis slipping past you, that is not a personal failing --- it is the predictable result of a culture in which postgraduates are sent to a one-week summer school and presumed competent, in which much is self-taught from scattered web searches, and in which supervisors are often no better placed than their students. The remedy is structural, not heroic: treat applied statistics as a core skill of the discipline, taught properly, rather than a bolt-on.

## Remedy 2: open data as part of the review process

Reviewers and editors can only catch what they can see. A look at the underlying data should be a standard part of review --- and reviewers should be equipped to make use of it. The clues in @WalkdenEa2023 as published are real but partial; the actual problems surface only on reanalysis. In our experience, reviewers --- even at empirically minded journals --- rarely catch design or analysis errors, whether for want of the data, want of the time to look, or want of the skills to look well. They tend instead to ask for more theoretical discussion, which rarely makes a paper's contribution any sounder.

Behind this sits a missing standard. Most journals will accept anything that reports a GLM, leaving quality assurance to the authors' discretion --- which, from the authors' side, is its own headache, since reviewers then impose whatever checks suit their taste. A journal with no best-practice guidelines for statistical methods arguably should not be publishing papers that lean on them at all, unless the paper's own contribution is methodological.

## Remedy 3: negative findings and preregistration

The pressure to publish, and to publish *positive*, is the engine underneath the whole problem. Rewriting @WalkdenEa2023 honestly --- "*we did not find evidence for Trudgill's theory, but we'll keep looking*" --- and getting it past reviewers would be a hard sell, and everyone knows it.

Preregistration is one answer [@Lakens2019]: the study's motivation and design are submitted and judged *before* it is run, and the paper is published on the strength of the design whatever the results turn out to be. That makes negative findings publishable and gives researchers room to be hard on their own data. We would welcome journals offering it --- but we are not convinced it solves much on its own. Negative results draw few citations, so the incentive to find something publishable survives, as does the temptation to wave a good-looking result through without inspecting the data or the model.^[Recent work suggests preregistration has to be done exactly right to curb the practices the positive-results pressure encourages [see, e.g., @BrodeurEa2024].] And in the present case the errors are elementary: the unweighted aggregated scores and the missing text-level random effects are the kind of thing a competent reviewer with the data in hand should catch in an afternoon.

We close on a constructive note rather than a sour one. Philology was once a discipline of careful close reading, aimed at understanding texts in their linguistic and cultural setting --- and, for good reason, it felt no obligation to the apparatus of the scientific method or to large-scale statistics. One reason was simply that the textual record is too thin, across the relevant times and places, to support reliable statistical inference. In many cases that has not really changed, and it is worth asking why quantitative analysis is so often reached for where a philological reading would serve better. None of this is a brief against statistics. The distinction that matters is the one Study 1 already turned on: describing a sample is one thing, inferring to a population another, and inferring to a causal network of hypotheses something else again. Exploratory data analysis is a genuine and valuable tool --- but its goals are orthogonal to *any* testing framework, principled or otherwise; it asks what is in the data, not whether a theory survives. Read that way, the data of @WalkdenEa2023 could have been put to good use. What sank the paper was not the statistics but the theory-confirmitis: exploratory-grade data marched through a confirmatory frame it could never satisfy. Match the instrument to what the data can bear --- close reading, exploration, or, where the data genuinely allow, a severe test --- and the quantitative turn might yet earn its keep.
